I found no error. I checked each step.
Step 1 (expanding V): the algebra is exact and every sum is finite.
Step 2 (counting pairs): pairs n<n' are exactly n'=n+hq. C_x(hq)=0 when hq>=x, and the case hq=x is kept in the sum consistently. This matters because D_x(m) is not zero for m>x, but those terms never enter the sum.
Divisibility lemma: t^2 | hq iff m_t(q) | h. Correct.
Interchange of the t- and h-sums: both sums are finite (t<=sqrt x), so the interchange is fine.
Arithmetic-progression sum: (X-θ)(X+θ-1)/2 = (X^2-X+B(X))/2 is correct, including when N=0, where B(X)=X-X^2 makes the bracket vanish. So t with q·m_t(q)>x correctly contribute 0.

Use of deps: P1(iv) and P1(v) are used exactly as stated, and 1/m_t(q)=gcd(t^2,q)/t^2 is correct.
Cancellation in Step 4: correct.
The statement is proved as stated, for all real x>=1 and all q, with no error terms.
Numerical check: I verified the identity in 30-digit arithmetic, with g taken from its exact Euler-product form and the MT tail for t>sqrt x handled exactly. Test cases: (x,q) = (200,7), (300,12), (150,1), (100,30), (97.5,5), (50.3,8), (3.7,2), (1,1), (40,100). The two sides agree to about 1e-27 in every case. This settles that the 1.5e-3 discrepancy reported in the proof's sanity check is truncation error, not an error in the identity.
